summary: Extends RSVP Graceful Restart for GMPLS so a restarting node can recover its signaling state from the Path message it last sent. Earlier mechanisms recovered state from neighbors when the data plane kept working. This extension covers more of the cases where a node restarts. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary:
RSVP is the protocol a router uses to reserve a path for traffic. If the router restarts, it can lose the record of which paths were set up. This RFC lets the router get that record back from the neighbour that received it, by having the neighbour send a copy of the Path message back.

The extension restores the signalling record only. The forwarding state that actually moves packets is not rebuilt, so it has to survive the restart on its own.

how do routers recover rsvp state after a restart
subtitle: Lets a router that has restarted rebuild its RSVP signalling state from the Path message its neighbour still holds.

tldr.problem: RSVP Graceful Restart lets a router that has restarted rebuild its signalling state, but the earlier mechanism only works when the data plane kept its forwarding state, and it cannot recover every object the router transmitted.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds a RecoveryPath message. A downstream neighbour sends it back to the restarted router, carrying a copy of the Path message it last received. A new Capability object in the RSVP Hello messages tells each side whether it can send and receive that message.
tldr.outcome: The restarted router can recover control plane state, including the Explicit Route Object and the downstream interface identifiers, without the data plane being rebuilt. A second mechanism, RecoveryPath Summary Refresh, lets the router ask only for the paths it could not rebuild itself.

today: RFC 5063 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 2961 and RFC 3473, and it defines the RecoveryPath message and the Capability object used by GMPLS RSVP-TE graceful restart.

sections.title: What This Extension Adds
sections.content:
RSVP Graceful Restart is defined in RFC 3473 and uses the mechanisms defined in RFC 3209. When the data and forwarding plane state of a router survives the restart of the RSVP agent that established it, that agent can resynchronise its own state from updates sent by its neighbouring RSVP agents, and reconcile that state with the forwarding state it kept.

That mechanism has two gaps, and this document closes both. It does not fully support signalling state recovery on ingress nodes, and it does not recover all RSVP objects. With these extensions the restarting node recovers every object it previously transmitted in a Path message, including the Explicit Route Object and the downstream interface identifiers, and the extensions also work when the node that restarts is an ingress node.

Two limits are stated at the start. The extensions are not used to create or restore data plane state, so they can only re-establish control plane state that matches forwarding state already in place. Restarting egress nodes and Resv message processing are not affected, and the extensions apply equally to LSPs of the various switching types described in RFC 3471.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP is how a router reserves a path for traffic. If the router restarts, it may lose the record of the paths it set up. This RFC lets the router recover that record by asking the neighbour downstream for a copy of the Path message it received. The router's forwarding state is not rebuilt; only the signalling record is restored.

sections.title: Control Plane, Data Plane and the Restart
sections.content:
Throughout this document, the term node, in the context of a restarting or restarted node, refers to the control plane component, which is the signalling controller for a data plane switch.

On a restart the node may lose the signalling state it built up. Some of that state can be rebuilt from the data plane. A restarting transit node consults the data plane to find its downstream interface and associated labels, and the presence of a Recovery Label object in the Path message from the upstream neighbour tells it that the Path message refers to existing forwarding state.

That is not always enough. Consulting the data plane may not be possible for all types of nodes, and data plane information is not sufficient to reconstruct all previously transmitted Path state. An ingress node has to recover all of its transmitted Path state, which can include the Protection object, the Admin Status object, the Session Attribute object, the Notify Request object and the Sender Tspec object. A transit node may have modified the Path state it received before passing it on, and that modification cannot be reconstructed internally during recovery. In those cases the downstream RSVP neighbour is the only source of RSVP state.
sections.plainLanguage: A router has two parts. The control plane decides which paths traffic may take. The data plane does the forwarding. After a restart the control plane may be empty while the data plane still knows where to send packets. This RFC restores the control plane's records from the neighbouring router, not the other way round.

sections.title: The RecoveryPath Message
sections.content:
A RecoveryPath message has the same format as a Path message, as defined in RFC 3473, but uses a new message number, 30, so that it can be identified correctly. The formal definition is <RecoveryPath Message> ::= <Path Message>.

The destination address used in the IP header of a RecoveryPath message MUST be the same as the destination address used in the IP header of the corresponding Resv message last generated by the sending node. Except for the exceptions below, all objects in a RecoveryPath message are identical to the objects in the corresponding Path message last received by the sending node.

Three kinds of object are handled differently. The MESSAGE_ID, MESSAGE_ID_ACK and MESSAGE_ID_NACK objects are not copied; any such objects used in RecoveryPath messages are generated based on the procedures of RFC 2961. The Integrity object is not copied, and any Integrity objects used are generated based on the procedures of RFC 2747. The RSVP Hop object is copied from the most recent associated Resv message sent to the restarted node for the LSP being recovered. In the sender descriptor, the Recovery Label object MUST be included, with the label value copied from the Label object in that same Resv message. All other objects from the most recent received Path message MUST be included in the RecoveryPath message.
sections.plainLanguage: The new message is a copy of a Path message, with one new message number so receivers recognise it. Three things are changed. The message identifiers are new. The integrity check is new. The hop and the recovery label come from the reservation message the neighbour sent earlier, so the restarted router learns which interface and label it had in use.

sections.title: The Capability Object in Hello Messages
sections.content:
Capability objects are carried in RSVP Hello messages. The Capability object uses Class-Number 134, of the form 10bbbbbb, and C-Type of 1. The Hello message format is modified to be:

<Hello Message> ::= <Common Header> [ <INTEGRITY> ] <HELLO> [ <RESTART_CAP> ] [ <CAPABILITY> ]

Three one-bit flags sit at the end of a 32-bit field, after 29 reserved bits. The reserved bits MUST be set to zero on transmission and MUST be ignored on receipt. The RecoveryPath Transmit Enabled (T) bit, when set to 1, indicates that the sending node is enabled to send RecoveryPath messages. The RecoveryPath Desired (R) bit, when set to 1, indicates that the sending node desires to receive RecoveryPath messages. The RecoveryPath Srefresh Capable (S) bit, when set to 1 together with the R bit, indicates that the sending node is capable of receiving and processing Srefresh messages with the RecoveryPath Flag set to 1 in the MESSAGE_ID LIST object. Absence of the Capability object MUST be treated as if all three bits are cleared.

Conformance rules follow. All nodes supporting these extensions MUST be able to transmit, and properly receive and process, RecoveryPath messages. All nodes MUST be able to set both the T and R bits, and both SHOULD be set to 1 by default. A node MAY allow RecoveryPath message transmission and reception to be independently disabled based on local policy. Any node that sets the Refresh-Reduction-Capable bit of RFC 2961 SHOULD support setting the S bit.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side advertises what it can do in the Hello messages the two routers exchange. Three flags cover the job: one says I can send these recovery messages, one says I want them, and one says I can also ask for them selectively. If a router does not send the object at all, the other router assumes all three flags are off.

sections.title: Sending and Handling RecoveryPath Messages
sections.content:
The downstream RSVP neighbour MUST send a RecoveryPath message for each LSP associated with the restarting node for which it has sent a Resv message, once it has detected that its upstream node has restarted, that the node is capable of recovery as defined in RFC 3473, and that it is capable of receiving RecoveryPath messages. All RecoveryPath messages SHOULD be sent at least once within approximately 1/2 of the Recovery Time advertised by the restarted neighbour. If there are many LSPs to be recovered, the neighbour should spread the messages across 1/2 the Recovery Time interval instead of sending them in a short interval, to avoid overloading the restarted node's CPU.

After sending a RecoveryPath message and during the Recovery Period, the sender SHOULD periodically resend it until it receives a corresponding response, which is a Message ID acknowledgment or a Path message for the LSP the RecoveryPath message represents. Each resend attempt MUST treat the RecoveryPath message as a new message and update the MESSAGE_ID object according to the procedures of RFC 2961. If the Message ID mechanism is not in use, the period between resend attempts SHOULD be such that at least 3 attempts are completed before the expiry of 3/4 the Recovery Time interval. Resv messages are suppressed during this period until a corresponding Path message is received.

The restarting node handles a RecoveryPath message during the Recovery Period by first checking whether it already has resynchronized RSVP state associated with the message. If it does, and reliable message delivery with a MESSAGE_ID object is supported, the node MUST follow the Message ID acknowledgment procedures and consider the message processed. If it does, but there is no MESSAGE_ID object or reliable message delivery is not supported, the node SHOULD send a trigger Path message and consider the message processed. If a non-resynchronized state is found, or the node is the ingress, the node saves the information in the RecoveryPath message and continues with the re-synchronization procedures.

Those procedures associate the recovered signalling state with forwarding state. The upstream data interface is recovered from the RSVP HOP object in the received Path message, and the upstream label from the Recovery Label object in that Path message. The downstream data interface is recovered from the RSVP HOP object in the RecoveryPath message, and the downstream label from the Recovery Label object in the RecoveryPath message. For a bidirectional LSP the label for the upstream direction comes from the Upstream Label object. If complete forwarding state is located, the restarted node MUST treat the LSP as resynchronized and MUST send a trigger Path message downstream. The Explicit Route object in that Path message SHOULD match the Explicit Route object received in the RecoveryPath message.

If no forwarding state is located, the node treats the received Path message as a setup request for a new LSP, and the outgoing interface and labels indicated in the RecoveryPath message SHOULD be reused when possible. Forwarding state MUST NOT be created except after receipt of a Path message from upstream or, at an ingress node, a command from the management plane, and the information received from downstream in the RecoveryPath message is treated only as advisory. At the end of the Recovery Period, any state installed as a result of a received RecoveryPath message that is not resynchronized SHOULD be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: After the restart, the neighbour sends back one recovery message for each reserved path, and keeps resending until it gets an answer. The restarted router matches the message against the forwarding state it still holds. If everything lines up, the path counts as recovered and the router sends a fresh Path message onward. If nothing lines up, the router treats it as a request for a new path, but it does not install forwarding state on its own.

sections.title: Working with Routers That Lack the Extension
sections.content:
This document introduces a new RSVP signalling message called the RecoveryPath message, generated by the downstream RSVP neighbour of a restarting node, and a new Capability object included in Hello messages by a restarting node and its downstream neighbours.

A restarting node that does not support the Capability object will discard it, as the Class-Number is of the form 10bbbbbb, and revert to recovery processing as defined in RFC 3473. It will not include the Capability object in its Hello messages, so every downstream neighbour that detects this treats the restarting node as not capable of supporting the extensions, does not send RecoveryPath messages, and reverts to the recovery processing of RFC 3473.

The same happens in the other direction. A downstream neighbour that does not support the Capability object discards the object received in Hello messages and reverts to recovery processing as defined in RFC 3473. It does not include the Capability object in its own Hello messages, so the restarting node detects that its neighbour cannot support the extensions and reverts as well.

Nothing else changes. The procedures for sending and receiving RSVP Hello messages, the Restart_Cap object, and the procedures for control channel faults are not modified, and the extensions address only nodal faults.
sections.plainLanguage: The object used to advertise the extension has a class number of a shape that older routers are required to ignore. So a router that does not know this extension simply behaves as before, and no recovery messages are sent. Either side can tell, from the Hello messages alone, whether the other understands.

sections.title: RecoveryPath Summary Refresh
sections.content:
This section describes a mechanism to control which LSP state is communicated in RecoveryPath messages. It enhances the Summary Refresh mechanism defined in RFC 2961 and uses the RecoveryPath Srefresh Capable (S) bit in the Capability object, carried in the Hello message. The mechanism is called RecoveryPath Summary Refresh.

In standard Summary Refresh, a node sends an Srefresh message to identify to its neighbour the Path and Resv state that is locally installed and available. The receiver attempts to locate matching state and, if none is found, requests the missing state by sending an Srefresh NACK. RecoveryPath Summary Refresh extends that process to the Path state that can be represented in RecoveryPath messages. The difference is that the Srefresh messages represent previously received Path messages rather than previously transmitted ones.

When a node restarts and is capable of supporting the mechanism, it includes the Capability object with both the R bit and the S bit set in its Hello messages. The neighbour then generates one or more Srefresh messages, each indicating the Path state that can be represented in a RecoveryPath message. The state is described with MESSAGE_ID information from the most recently received Path message, carried in MESSAGE_ID LIST objects. To mark this, a new bit is defined in the existing Flags field of the MESSAGE_ID LIST, MESSAGE_ID_ACK and MESSAGE_ID_NACK objects. The RecoveryPath Flag has the value 0x02 in the 8-bit Flags field, and the same flag value is used in all the objects for consistency.

The restarted node uses the Epoch and Message ID tuples in the Srefresh message to match against the Path messages it transmitted downstream before the restart. Where matching state is located, the node treats the corresponding LSP state as recovered and MUST generate a trigger Path message, which it MAY spread across 1/2 of the remaining Recovery Period. Where no matching state is located, the node MUST generate a MESSAGE_ID NACK with the RecoveryPath Flag set, and the downstream neighbour then generates a RecoveryPath message for the Path state indicated by each entry in the MESSAGE_ID LIST. Path state whose MESSAGE_ID object has an Epoch matching the Epoch in the most recent Hello message is considered updated after the upstream neighbour restarted, and such state MUST NOT be represented in the Srefresh messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending every recovered path back can be a lot of traffic, so the restarted router can ask for only the ones it is missing. The neighbour answers with a list of message identifiers; the router matches them against what it remembers. Anything it cannot match, it asks for by name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document introduces a new RSVP message that is restricted to one RSVP hop, and a new RSVP object to be included in RSVP Hello messages. It introduces no new security considerations beyond those already addressed for existing RSVP hop-by-hop messages and for existing objects in RSVP Hello messages.

The procedures assume a full trust model between RSVP neighbours. The protocol exchanges before and after a restart can be secured, and it is possible to authenticate the identity of the neighbours, but no mechanism is provided to verify that the restart information is correctly mapped from the protocol information exchanged before the restart. This is considered acceptable because a similar trust model is required for normal operation of the protocol.

One property is stated as a safety rule. The procedures cannot be used to create false forwarding state: a restarting node that receives a RecoveryPath message which does not match the existing forwarding state MUST NOT create or modify its forwarding state to match, and SHOULD log such an event or otherwise notify the operator, since it might represent an attack. The mechanisms of RFC 2747, when used with the new message and procedures, provide the same degree of protection against installing compromised signalling state during recovery.

The procedures also add processing overhead to the RSVP agents that neighbour a restarting agent. That impact can be minimised by the restarting agent using a large enough Recovery Time, so that its neighbours have sufficient time to handle the additional processing while continuing their other control plane functions during the Recovery Period.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighbours of a restarting router are assumed to trust each other. The messages can be protected in transit, but there is no check that the information handed back after the restart really matches what was sent before it. One rule limits the damage: a router that receives a recovery message which does not match its forwarding state must not change its forwarding state to fit it, and should log the event.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: RecoveryPath Transmit Enabled (T)
fields.desc: Set when the node may send RecoveryPath messages.

fields.name: RecoveryPath Desired (R)
fields.desc: Set when the node wants to receive RecoveryPath messages.

fields.name: RecoveryPath Srefresh Capable (S)
fields.desc: Set with R when the node can process RecoveryPath Srefresh messages.

viz.caption: RECOVERY OF ONE PATH AFTER A RESTART

messages.label: PATH
messages.note: Sent before the restart. The neighbour keeps a copy.

messages.label: PATH WITH RECOVERY LABEL
messages.note: Tells the restarted node that this Path message refers to existing forwarding state.

messages.label: HELLO WITH R BIT
messages.note: The restarted node asks to receive RecoveryPath messages.

messages.label: HELLO WITH T BIT
messages.note: The neighbour says it is enabled to send them.

messages.label: RECOVERYPATH
messages.note: A copy of the last Path message the neighbour received.

messages.label: PATH (TRIGGER)
messages.note: Sent once the restarted node has matched the message to forwarding state.
